_note: Single source of truth for plain-language explanations. Consumed by: hover tooltips ('short'), the Reader's guide ('long'), and the assistant via the Worker. Rewritten for the October 2026 release; describes only what is on the portal.

terms.short: The grid on the Structure page. Each row is a source variable, each column a receiver; a colored square is a relationship from that row to that column, blue if positive, red if negative, shaded by its causal score.
terms.long: An adjacency matrix is a compact way to display a network. Every variable appears as a row (acting as a source), and every variable that can receive an influence appears as a column. A colored cell at row i, column j means the model retained a relationship from variable i to variable j: blue if the influence is positive, red if negative, with the shade giving the causal score. Weakly signed relationships are muted grey. Blank cells mean no retained relationship; the diagonal is hatched. Structural variables appear as rows only, since nothing is estimated into them. Variables are ordered so that strongly linked ones sit together; the faint lines mark groups, which are an aid to reading and not statistically distinct clusters. Hovering any cell shows the two variable names, the score with its range across fits, the sign, and the sign's strength; clicking a row or column label opens that variable's neighborhood view.

terms.short: Nodes are the variables in the model; edges are the directed relationships between them, each running from a source to a receiver with a sign and a score.
terms.long: The model is a network. Nodes are its variables: some single V-Dem indicators, some factors that combine several indicators, some composites. Edges are directed relationships: an edge from A to B means A's recent past improves the prediction of B's next value, given everything else. Direction matters, and an edge from A to B does not imply one from B to A. Each edge carries a causal score, a sign, a sign strength, and the number of fits in which it was kept. The Edges view lists every retained edge; the Structure view shows the same information as a matrix.

terms.short: For any edge, the source is the variable doing the influencing and the receiver is the variable whose forecast it improves. Rows are sources, columns are receivers.
terms.long: Every edge has a direction. The source is the variable whose recent past contributes to the prediction; the receiver (or target) is the variable being predicted. In the adjacency matrix, rows are sources and columns are receivers, so reading across a row shows everything that variable influences, and reading down a column shows everything that influences it. Structural variables act only as sources.

terms.short: The panel that opens when you click a variable name: its definition, its member indicators if it is a factor, and every edge into and out of it, as a table or as a network.
terms.long: Clicking any variable label in the adjacency matrix opens its neighborhood view. This shows the variable's name and code, its kind, its member indicators if it is a factor or composite, and every incoming and outgoing edge with sign and score, as a table or as a small network in which the variable's neighbors are placed near the ones they are linked to. For a factor, the member list is the authoritative definition of what the factor measures.

terms.term: The two panels (Century and Modern views)
terms.short: Two separate analyses: the Century view (1900–2023, 169 countries, V-Dem only, 59 nodes) and the Modern view (1970–2021, 150 countries, V-Dem plus economic, demographic and globalization data, 81 nodes). They are never merged.
terms.long: The portal presents two independent analyses, selectable at the top of the page. The Century view covers 1900 to 2023 using V-Dem indicators alone, trading breadth of variables for historical depth. The Modern view covers 1970 to 2021 and adds World Bank, UN population, KOF globalization and Maddison Project measures, trading historical reach for richer covariates. Each panel has its own variables, its own factors, its own estimated structure and its own forecasts; quantities are not comparable across them, and factor numbering does not correspond.

terms.short: The causal model is fitted three times from different random starting points. Edges kept in all three fits form the consensus graph (the default); edges kept in two of three are shown as majority edges when toggled on.
terms.long: Neural models depend partly on their random starting point, so a relationship found by one fit could be an artifact of it. The estimation is therefore repeated three times. An edge is retained if it passes the selection tests in at least two fits; those passing in all three form the consensus graph, the portal's default and the object the papers treat as canonical. Majority-only edges are plausible but less stable and are drawn faded or dashed. Scores are reported as the median across fits with the range beside it.

terms.short: How many years ahead a forecast or a what-if response is read: 1, 3, 5 or 10. The first three are validated; ten years is published without validation.
terms.long: Horizon counts years forward from the year a forecast is made. Forecasts are issued at 1, 3, 5 and 10 years. Forecasts at 1, 3 and 5 years have been checked against what was then observed; the 10-year horizon is published without validation because too few ten-year outcomes have been observed yet, and it is labelled as such wherever it appears.

terms.short: Varieties of Democracy, the expert-coded dataset behind this portal: hundreds of indicators of democratic institutions and practices from 1789 onward. This portal uses version 15.
terms.long: V-Dem (Varieties of Democracy) is a research project based at the University of Gothenburg producing the largest available dataset on democracy. It measures hundreds of specific attributes of political systems, most coded by multiple country experts and combined through a measurement model that accounts for coder disagreement. This portal uses V-Dem version 15. Variable codes beginning v2 are V-Dem indicators; codes beginning KOF, wb or wpp are from the additional sources used in the Modern panel.

terms.short: Several indicators that measure the same concept, combined into one variable by confirmatory factor analysis, specified from theory. Each factor displays its construct name; its member indicators define it.
terms.long: V-Dem measures some concepts with many closely related indicators. Entering them separately would make the unit of analysis an indicator rather than a concept, so indicators that measure the same concept are combined by confirmatory factor analysis: which indicators belong to which construct is fixed in advance from theory, and each factor is scored by its best linear unbiased predictor. The century panel has eight factors (civil liberties, engagement in independent associations, party institutionalization, politicized judiciary, autocratic legitimacy, academic freedom, corruption and inclusive development); the modern panel has the same eight and eight more drawn from economic and demographic data. Factor numbering is panel-specific.

terms.short: A single variable built from a set of categories that sum to a whole, re-expressed as log-ratios so the parts can be analyzed without the dependence a fixed total creates.
terms.long: A few V-Dem items are recorded as shares across categories that add up to one. Shares like that cannot be analyzed as independent numbers, because raising one must lower the others. They are re-expressed as log-ratios, the standard treatment for compositional data, and enter the model as one variable. Both panels have two such composites.

terms.short: Variables, such as land area, that differ between countries but barely change within them. They may influence others but no relationship is estimated into them and they are not forecast.
terms.long: Some variables vary almost entirely between countries rather than within a country over time. The intraclass correlation measures this: the share of a variable's variance that lies between countries. A variable with more than 90% of its variance between countries is treated as structural. It can act as a source in the causal structure, but no relationship is estimated into it, it is not forecast, and it is not moved in the what-if view, because it does not make large moves. The century panel has no structural variables; the modern panel has 16, shown as a band of rows at the bottom of the matrix with no columns of their own.

terms.short: The model behind the causal structure: it predicts each variable's next value from the last three years of every variable, with each source making a separate, flexibly shaped contribution that can be examined on its own.
terms.long: NAVAR predicts each variable's next value from the last three years of every variable. Each source passes through its own small neural network and makes a separate contribution to each receiver; the prediction is the sum of those contributions. A contribution can take any shape, so thresholds and saturation are allowed, while the additive form keeps each source's influence separately visible. An influence in this sense is causal as Granger defined it: the source's recent past improves the prediction of the receiver's next value, given the recent past of everything else. It is not a claim about what an intervention would do.

terms.short: The size of a source's influence on a receiver: the standard deviation of its contribution across the data. It measures size, not direction; the sign is assigned separately.
terms.long: Each edge's causal score is the standard deviation across the data of the source's contribution to the receiver's prediction: how much that contribution moves. Scores are reported as the median across the three fits, with the min-max range beside it, and are compared within a panel, not across panels. A score measures the size of an influence only; its direction is given by the edge's sign.

terms.short: An edge is kept only if removing the source's contribution reliably worsens the receiver's prediction (false discovery rate held at 5%), if it falls in the group of large effects, and if this holds in at least two of three fits.
terms.long: A fitted model assigns some contribution to every pair of variables, so a test is needed for which contributions matter. First, forecast necessity: the source's contribution is removed and the rise in the receiver's prediction error is measured; a one-sided Diebold-Mariano test asks whether the rise is reliable, and the false discovery rate across all pairs is held at 5%. Second, dominance: among the edges that pass, the error increases fall into a mass of small effects and a group of large ones; a two-component mixture model separates them and the large group is kept. Third, replication across three fits.

terms.short: Each edge is positive (blue) or negative (red) according to the direction of its effect curve, by majority across the three fits. Edges whose effect reverses direction across the source's range (shape SC) have no single direction and are drawn in grey.
terms.long: A causal score says how large an influence is, not which way it goes. The sign is taken from the direction in which the source's contribution moves with the source's latest value, decided by majority across the three fits. Sign strength, from 0 to 1, says how consistently the effect runs in one direction. Where the effect curve reverses direction across the source's range the edge is classified as sign-changing (code SC) and shown in grey rather than blue or red; the effect curve is the full picture for any edge. Signs describe the causal structure one year ahead; the what-if responses in the forecaster are a different object and do not confirm or test them.

terms.short: For a consensus edge, the receiver's predicted value as the source is moved across its observed range with everything else held as observed. Shows the shape of a relationship, which a score or sign cannot.
terms.long: For each consensus edge, the receiver's predicted value is traced as the source is moved across its observed range, with everything else held as observed: an individual conditional expectation curve. It shows whether a relationship is steady, has a threshold, or saturates. Curves are drawn for three groups of country-years, the lower, middle and upper thirds of the clean elections index. Because the model is additive, the three curves of an edge share one shape and differ by a constant; the split shows where each group's typical values lie on the curve, not different effects in different groups. Axes are in standardized units; the grid spans the 2nd to 98th percentile of the source's observed values.

terms.short: Variables in the matrix are ordered so that strongly linked ones sit together, using community detection made stable across repeated runs. The groups are an aid to reading, not statistically distinct clusters.
terms.long: The order of rows and columns in the adjacency matrix is chosen so that variables with strong links appear near one another, using modularity-based community detection made stable by consensus across repeated runs. The faint lines mark the resulting groups. They are an ordering, not a finding: the caption reports the modularity of the ordering beside the modularity of randomly rewired graphs with the same density, and on both panels the two are close.

terms.short: The letter in each matrix cell summarizes the effect curve: L linear, ST saturating (levels off at high values of the source), T threshold (switches on at high values), N nonlinear, SC sign-changing (reverses direction), M mixed (the three fits disagree).
terms.long: Each relationship's effect curve is classified by its shape. L, linear: about equally steep across the source's range. ST, saturating: the effect levels off as the source rises. T, threshold: the effect is absent until the source passes some level. N, nonlinear: one-directional and curved, but neither saturating nor threshold. SC, sign-changing: the effect reverses direction over the source's range, so the edge has no single direction and is drawn in grey. M, mixed: the three fitted models give three different shapes; it is a disagreement, not a seventh kind of relationship. The code is a summary of the fitted curve the Effect curves view draws; the hover shows how many of the three fits agree on it. 'Low' and 'high' refer to the source's value.

terms.short: One spatio-temporal graph neural network serves all countries, forecasting every dynamic variable 1, 3, 5 and 10 years ahead as a distribution. It starts from a no-change forecast and learns adjustments to it.
terms.long: The forecaster is a spatio-temporal graph neural network with one set of weights for all countries, so a pattern learned from one country's history is available when the model reads another's. It reads each country's level and one-year change of every variable over the previous 30 years (century) or 20 years (modern), updates each country's state with information from neighbours within 100 km, trading partners weighted by trade share, and countries it learns to associate, and lets each variable read its own last three years through a function of its own. It starts from a no-change forecast and learns adjustments to it, so an untrained model reproduces no change exactly. The published forecast averages six independently trained copies. Forecasts are made only with information available in the year they are issued; the model is refitted at 2000, 2005, 2010 and 2015.

terms.short: A forecast is a distribution reported as its 5th, 25th, 50th, 75th and 95th percentiles. The median is the point forecast; the outer percentiles give a nominal 90% band, which in the evaluation period held the outcome 80 to 87% of the time.
terms.long: Each forecast is estimated as five percentiles by quantile regression. The median (50th) is the point forecast. The 25th to 75th percentiles are the middle half. The 5th to 95th percentiles form a nominal 90% band: nominal because its realized coverage in the evaluation period was 80 to 87% at 1, 3 and 5 years, so it under-covers somewhat and is not calibrated. The portal says so wherever the band appears.

terms.short: The reference every forecast is judged against: the assumption that the variable stays at its last observed value. These variables change slowly, so no change is hard to beat.
terms.long: A no-change forecast assumes each variable stays at its last observed value. Because democratic institutions change slowly, no change is close to the outcome most of the time, and any forecast, including the model's, scores well in absolute terms. Accuracy is therefore meaningful only beside this reference. The forecast's margin over no change is small and narrows with horizon, and for some variables the point forecast is behind no change; the full forecast distribution is further ahead than the point forecast.

terms.term: Accuracy: MAE and error as % of range
terms.short: The headline measure is the mean absolute error (MAE) of the forecast median against what was observed, in the variable's own units, shown beside the MAE of a no-change forecast. Error as a percentage of the variable's observed range makes it comparable across variables.
terms.long: Every forecast made in 2006 or later is compared with the value then observed. MAE, the average absolute gap between the forecast median and the outcome, is the headline measure because it is defined for every variable and easy to read; it is always shown beside the MAE of a no-change forecast. Error as a percentage of the variable's observed range puts variables with different units on one footing. A country figure is shown only where at least three forecasts could be scored. The whole distribution is also scored (continuous ranked probability score, as a ratio to no change) and the bands by their realized coverage; those figures are in the methods text.

terms.short: A large move is a change of more than half a standard deviation of the variable's own level. For each variable, country and horizon a second model estimates the probability of a large fall and a large rise.
terms.long: Democratic change is punctuated: long periods of little movement broken by short periods of large movement. A large move is defined as a change of more than half a standard deviation of a variable's own level over the horizon. A second model with the same inputs as the forecaster divides each variable's historical changes into large falls, large rises and everything else, and learns how likely each is given a country's current situation. Fall probabilities are informative at every validated horizon; rise probabilities at one year and only weakly beyond.

terms.short: The change in a forecast when one variable is different today: the forecaster is asked again with that variable moved by half a standard deviation, up or down. It is a statement about prediction, not an estimate of a causal effect.
terms.long: To show what would change a forecast, the forecaster is asked again. A country's latest observed data are taken, a large move is applied to one variable, everything else is left as observed, and the change in the forecast median of every other variable is read at each horizon. A variable is moved only in a direction in which at least 20 such one-year moves have been observed, structural variables are never moved, one country is changed at a time, and each horizon is forecast directly. A response is the change in a prediction when one condition is different today; it is not an estimate of what an intervention would do, and it does not confirm or test the signs in the Structure view. Responses are generally small, a large move mostly persists, and countries differ a great deal, which is why the view opens on one country.
